data.title: Vanta Closes Second Tranche of Private Placement Financing and Welcomes Launch of First U.S.-Listed Peptide ETF, Highlighting Growing Recognition of Peptide Industry
data.description:
VANCOUVER, BC / ACCESS Newswire / October 16, 2026 / Vanta Holdings Inc. (FSE:7BC, WKN:A4205J) ("Vanta" or the "Company"), a consumer health sciences and longevity company focused on preventative wellness and healthspan extension, and parent of the Vanta premium longevity brand, announces that, further to its news releases dated May 29, 2026, and August 21, 2026, the Company has closed, effective October 15, 2026, the second tranche (the "Second Tranche") of its previously announced non-brokered private placement (the "Private Placement"), through the issuance of 210,000 units of the Company (each, a "Unit") at a price of $1.00 per Unit, for aggregate gross proceeds of $210,000. Each Unit consists of one common share in the capital of the Company (each, a "Share") and one transferable common share purchase warrant (each, a "Warrant"). Each Warrant entitles the holder to acquire one additional Share (each, a "Warrant Share") at an exercise price of $1.25 per Warrant Share, exercisable until October 15, 2028.

The securities issued under the Private Placement will be subject to a statutory hold period expiring February 17, 2027. In connection with the closing of the Second Tranche, the Company paid aggregate cash finder's fees of $1,500 to registered dealers.

The net proceeds of the Private Placement are intended to be allocated towards the payment of outstanding and future payables and indebtedness, including amounts owing to related parties, and corporate awareness.

Together with the closing of the first tranche of the Private Placement, the Company has raised aggregate gross proceeds of C$334,579.42 through the issuance of an aggregate of 334,579 Units pursuant to the Private Placement. The Second Tranche constitutes the final tranche of the Private Placement.

This press release shall not constitute an offer to sell or the solicitation of an offer to buy securities in the United States, nor shall there be any sale of the securities in any jurisdiction in which such offer, solicitation or sale would be unlawful. The securities being offered have not been, nor will they be, registered under the U.S. Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the "1933 Act"), or under any U.S. state securities laws, and may not be offered or sold in the United States absent registration or an applicable exemption from the registration requirements of the 1933 Act and applicable state securities laws.

Launch of First U.S.-Listed Peptide ETF

The Company welcomes the October 14, 2026 launch of the Nasdaq-listed REX Peptide ETF by REX Shares. Described by its sponsor as the first U.S.-listed pure-play peptide exchange-traded fund, the ETF provides diversified exposure to companies engaged in the development, manufacturing, delivery and commercialization of peptide-based products. It tracks the VettaFi Peptide Index, which comprised 36 constituents as of September 30, 2026.

Vanta believes the introduction of a dedicated peptide ETF reflects growing recognition of peptide-based innovation across a broad range of therapeutic, healthcare and consumer wellness applications. The Company is not affiliated with REX Shares or the REX Peptide ETF, and the ETF's launch does not imply any investment in, endorsement of, or commercial relationship with Vanta.

Vanta's Position in the Evolving Peptide Industry

Vanta has established a strategic operating framework and infrastructure relationships to support its planned U.S.-focused peptide platform. As disclosed in its news release dated May 28, 2026, the Company, through its indirect wholly-owned subsidiary, Vanta Amino Sciences Incorporated, entered into a master services, commercialization and strategic operations agreement with an arm's-length strategic operating partner.

The agreement establishes a framework for coordinating compounding pharmacy relationships, peptide manufacturing and fulfillment capabilities, compliant payment processing infrastructure, and telehealth-enabled commercialization support. Commercialization remains subject to adequate funding, compliance with applicable regulatory requirements, and the execution of definitive commercial agreements, as applicable.

The planned platform complements Vanta's existing nutraceutical and premium functional hydration portfolio and forms part of its broader consumer health sciences and longevity strategy.

About Vanta Holdings Inc.

Vanta Holdings Inc. (FSE:7BC0, WKN:A4205J) is a consumer health sciences and longevity company advancing an integrated ecosystem of U.S.-focused peptide therapy, nutraceutical, and premium hydration products centered on preventative wellness and healthspan extension, positioning the Company to participate in the rapidly expanding longevity economy.

Vanta is advancing a U.S.-focused telehealth-enabled peptide therapy and longevity platform leveraging commercialization infrastructure and FDA-registered 503A and 503B compounding pharmacy relationships to pursue initiatives across recovery, metabolic wellness, performance optimization, and healthy aging categories.

Through its Vanta brand and select private-label partnerships, the Company develops, manufactures, and distributes premium hydration and longevity-oriented nutraceutical products, including, without limitation, its flagship proprietary Blackwater and BlackPowder product portfolio featuring bioactive compounds, trace mineral complexes, and patented Fulvic Isolation Technology™ designed to support hydration, mineral replenishment, cellular function, immune function, gut health, nutrient absorption, cognitive function, and broader everyday wellness-focused applications aligned with growing consumer demand for functional health optimization products. Vanta's vertically integrated operations include ownership of a natural alkaline spring water aquifer and a 40,000-square-foot, Health Canada and HACCP-certified manufacturing facility situated in the mountains of British Columbia.

data.title: Former Ripple Adviser Warns XRP’s Biggest Test Is Still Ahead
data.description:
Former Ripple CBDC adviser Anthony Welfare told the AllinCrypto Podcast that the XRP Ledger (XRPL) has strong technical features. Those strengths alone will not guarantee adoption.

Institutions are testing the network, and a new Nasdaq listing has put XRP in front of stock investors.

What the XRP Ledger Brings to Finance

The XRPL’s features suit payments and tokenization, but Welfare argues technology is only part of the picture. Several practical questions determine whether institutions actually use it.

“When you see a lot of the things that are put out about XRP and its kind of ecosystem and Ripple as a company, and to set the stage even further there, it being this kind of like new financial system that can solve correspondent banking and that everybody can do all these use cases on and that our new financial system can run upon,” Welfare said.

Welfare’s main points are:

  • Speed, low costs, and a native decentralized exchange suit payments and tokenization well.
  • The XRP asset differs from the XRP Ledger, so institutions can use ledger functions without relying on the token.
  • Liquidity, custody, compliance, and interoperability bridge technical readiness and real-world use.
  • “The tech is there,” he said, citing his work advising central banks and on payment projects.
  • Private blockchains will likely expand first, with some activity later anchoring to public networks.

He also sees a role for auditable records that AI agents can rely on, which calls for trusted transaction layers. Stablecoins could reduce payment friction and create new orchestration opportunities for existing players, rather than eliminating them.

Is Recent Momentum Enough to Drive Adoption?

Developments over the past month lend support to that view. A European consortium is targeting euro stablecoin adoption across several networks, including the XRP Ledger.

That multi-network approach fits Welfare’s view of a multi-chain future. Welfare sees interoperability, rather than dominance by one chain, as the key commercial opportunity.

The IMF has mapped the XRP Ledger alongside other public ledgers in discussions of tokenized finance. Ripple has also expanded partnerships, including Ripple Prime services for Brevan Howard.

An integration with DriveWealth uses RLUSD on the XRP Ledger to speed up global funding. Each development shows the ledger in a different role, from settlement to funding.

Evernorth, a Ripple-backed vehicle holding about 473 million XRP, debuted on Nasdaq under the ticker XRPN this week. Shares opened at $16.68, briefly climbed to $19.38, and closed at $16.91 on Monday, October 12.

On Wednesday, October 14, XRPN closed at $15.26, down 7.40%. That gives traditional investors stock-market exposure to a large XRP treasury, without buying tokens directly.

Against that backdrop, XRP price is up 1.72% over the past 24 hours, according to BeInCrypto data. It trades near $1.34 as of mid-October, and price action remains volatile.

Even so, whether this institutional activity becomes lasting demand remains an open question.

data.title: Bangladesh is battling measles. It's a 'real warning' to other nations
data.description:
Key points:
  • After years of successes, vaccination programme faltered in 2025
  • Bangladesh reported 202,000 cases, 1,147 deaths 2026 so far
  • Emergency inoculation rollout missed out millions, data shows
  • Poor 'pay the price' when preparation falls short, says expert
  • Government promises to reach all children, WHO pledges support

By Ruma Paul, Jennifer Rigby, Sam Jahan and Zia Chowdhury

Bangladesh is battling to contain the world’s worst measles outbreak, a crisis exacerbated by weak data, inadequate outreach and vaccination gaps that experts say offers a warning to other nations about the deadly risk of falling immunisation rates.

Bangladesh, whose routine vaccination programme faltered in 2025, reported 202,000 suspected measles cases – 22,000 of them laboratory-confirmed – since the start of the outbreak in mid-March to October 9, the World Health Organization said. That’s more suspected cases than any other country this year.

So far, 1,147 people have died of the highly contagious disease, with 94% of reported deaths among children under five years old, the WHO said.

Bangladesh's experience shows the challenge of containing an outbreak when vaccination coverage falls below 95%, a level the WHO says is needed to prevent outbreaks. Bangladesh almost achieved that in recent years but in 2025 coverage dropped.

A Reuters review of WHO documents, alongside interviews with more than a dozen scientists, health workers and officials, shows Bangladesh was also hampered in its emergency response by data that left out millions of children, shortcomings in preparation and a failure to reach enough parents.

"This is a real warning to every country," said Mark Jit, a WHO vaccine adviser and professor at the School of Global Public Health at New York University.

Preventing an outbreak through vaccinations was easier, cheaper and safer than responding to an emergency, he said.

"The response will stop the outbreak eventually, but in the meantime, many will have had measles, and some will have died," he said.

Ziauddin Hyder, special assistant on health affairs to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, told Reuters in September the government was doing everything it could to end the outbreak. The government did not respond to further questions sent in October for this article.

‘THEY CAME ONLY AFTER I BURIED MY SON’

In the northeast Sylhet region, one of the worst-hit areas in the nation of 178 million people, two-year-old Arman Hossain died unvaccinated in July, 24 hours after admission to hospital for treatment paid for by selling the family's three-wheeled auto rickshaw. His unvaccinated four-year-old sister survived.

His father Amin Mia, 26, said no health workers came to their remote village in Sylhet to offer vaccinations in time. "They came only after I buried my son," he said.

Measles usually kills two or three people in every 1,000 cases, the WHO says, but the disease can be more deadly in poorer nations because of factors such as malnutrition.

In the town of Chhatak, also in the Sylhet region, the daughter of 30-year-old carpenter Humayun Rashid died unvaccinated in June aged nine months. Labiba Akter could have received an inoculation in April when an emergency programme lowered the vaccination age to six months from nine.

"No health worker came to tell us," her father said.

In May, Health Minister Sardar Md. Sakhawat Husain said the emergency drive had brought cases in hotspots "almost to zero" and the outbreak was under control.

Yet in September, Bangladesh reported a daily average of 1,198 new cases of measles, which causes a high fever, cough and telltale rash. That was the highest total since May.

The Bangladesh outbreak comes as vaccine hesitancy is rising, particularly in wealthier nations, amid skepticism championed by figures such as US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

In Bangladesh, access to inoculations and awareness are bigger hurdles, experts said.

Until recently, Bangladesh had been a vaccination success story. The WHO and the United Nations children’s agency UNICEF estimated that in 2024 it achieved 96% coverage for the first vaccine dose and 93% for the second, which is given to capture the small percentage of children who don't develop immunity after one shot.

But that same year, protests erupted that ended 15 years of rule by Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. In the ensuing political turmoil, health workers went on strike, vaccine orders were delayed and follow-up vaccinations that usually accompany routine programmes were disrupted.

In a report published in July this year, WHO and UNICEF estimated first-dose coverage in 2025 had fallen to 90%, while second-dose coverage was 86%, several percentage points below the 95% needed for herd immunity.

The report also raised questions about the quality of official data on vaccinations for measles and other diseases for the years 2023 to 2025.

It said preliminary figures sometimes showed numbers of those inoculated exceeded 100% of those targeted, indicating mistakes in counting doses or target numbers.

EMERGENCY PROGRAMME MISSED MILLIONS

Still, when the measles outbreak erupted, Bangladesh responded swiftly and initially seemed to be winning the battle.

An emergency programme was followed by an initial slowdown in new cases after almost 20 million children received a vaccination in April and May. The government said it had covered every child in the target age group of six months to five years.

But in reality the programme fell short. This emerged when another routine health intervention in June had a target list with 4 million more children than the measles campaign despite covering the same age group.

"There is a gap," prime ministerial adviser Hyder told Reuters on September 14, as measles cases rose again, blaming vaccine hesitancy by parents or child illnesses for keeping kids away.

Other challenges have also emerged.

Documents detailing meetings in April and August between the government, the WHO and other health partners, reviewed by Reuters and not previously reported, show how efforts to act fast may have led to shortcomings.

Minutes from the April 19 meeting outlined how the government opted for just one round of so-called readiness checks before launching its emergency vaccination programme due to time constraints, instead of the typical four rounds. Checks cover everything from ensuring fridges are available for keeping vaccines cool to determining how many children should be vaccinated.

The single round of checks suggested most - but not all - districts were ready, according to the minutes.

THE POOREST ‘PAY THE PRICE’

"When preparedness checks are not done properly, it is often the poorest and hardest-to-reach children who miss out on vaccination and pay the price," said Professor Mahmudur Rahman, an epidemiologist and chair of Bangladesh's National Verification Committee for Measles and Rubella Elimination.

Hyder said the April campaign was launched in four weeks. Yet Tajul Islam Abdul Bari, who led immunisation in Bangladesh until 2017, said campaigns usually demand months of planning.

By the August meeting, shortcomings in the rollout were identified. Minutes noted the proportion of children with confirmed measles cases who had not been vaccinated was "virtually unchanged between pre-campaign (82%) and post-campaign (85%) ... underscoring persistent coverage gaps".

The WHO did not respond to questions about the April and August meetings. But deputy WHO representative to Bangladesh, Dr Rajesh Narwal, said the WHO was determined to support the government in its goal of vaccinating every child at risk.

"Routine immunisation must become more effective and resilient so that these gaps do not develop again," he said.

In Sylhet, where official records show 180 children have died, 8 of 16 families Reuters interviewed in September said they had not seen health workers offering vaccinations. At least six families said health workers visited only after a child had died from measles in their community.

At the end of September, the government launched a new campaign to target 3.4 million children previously missed.

"We will involve people across villages so that no child is left behind," the health minister told a news conference.

Yet reaching every child remains a challenge. UNICEF and the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics say as many as 40% of children go unregistered, while government data showed around a third of health worker posts are unfilled.

Health experts are also pushing the government to expand the programme to vaccinate children over five. That age group represents a third of measles cases, the WHO says.

In addition, scientists in Bangladesh are studying why immunity is waning faster than expected in babies up to six months or so. They are usually still protected by maternal antibodies, experts say.

Ensuring prompt medical care is vital, the WHO says, another challenge for Bangladesh as it also fights a dengue epidemic.

In September, every ward in Sylhet's 100-bed Shahid Shamsuddin Ahmed Hospital, which is treating measles, appeared overwhelmed. On the day Reuters visited, 178 patients were admitted.

data.title: US holds more secret talks with Myanmar's military-backed rulers in Tokyo, sources say
data.description:
Key points:
  • Second round of US-Myanmar talks in a month
  • Outreach marks sharp reversal since 2021 coup
  • US focused on Myanmar's scam hubs, eyes rare earths
  • Japan also tentatively re-engaging with isolated regime

By Simon Lewis, Poppy McPherson and John Geddie

The US and Myanmar's military-backed government held talks in Tokyo last week, people familiar with the matter said, their second meeting in a month as Washington steps up re-engagement with the generals it shunned after their 2021 coup.

Earlier talks in Myanmar's capital Naypyitaw in mid-September focused on securing the release of an American businessman and shutting down scam centers that target Americans, but could pave the way for broader discussions, including on Myanmar’s rare-earth mineral deposits, Reuters previously reported.

It was not immediately clear exactly what the two sides discussed at last week's talks, disclosed to Reuters by three people with knowledge of the engagement. The people, including one US official, all requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the meeting.

US Assistant Secretary of ​State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance again led the Tokyo talks, which involved more than a dozen US officials, one of the people said. Reuters could not establish who represented Myanmar.

A US official disputed that Vance is leading US policy toward Myanmar. "In coordination with other agencies, the State Department has a wide range of officials that lead on Burma policy," the US official said, using the country's former name.

The Trump administration says it engages with all ⁠groups in Myanmar on issues affecting US interests. A spokesperson for Myanmar's military-backed government did not ​respond to a request for comment.

Asked about its role in hosting the talks, Japan's Foreign Ministry said in an emailed statement it had been "communicating as necessary" with both sides but declined to comment on specific diplomatic exchanges.

Last month's meeting in Naypyitaw between Vance and Myanmar's coup leader-turned-president, Min Aung Hlaing, provided an opening for broader discussions, people familiar with those talks previously told Reuters. The quick return to the negotiating table in Tokyo suggests both sides are keen to keep the dialogue going.

A major focus of the US push is securing Myanmar's help in shutting down scam hubs that run romance and other frauds and have swindled Americans out of billions of dollars, the people said.

Researchers say many scam operations are based in areas controlled by army-backed militia, with some proceeds flowing to the military, raising doubts about whether Myanmar's leaders are serious about enforcement. Myanmar's military-backed government has said it is participating in a multinational effort to curb scam centres.

US officials have also discussed access to Myanmar's large deposits of heavy rare earths, which are used in products ranging from electric vehicles to wind turbines. US officials acknowledge significant obstacles: the deposits are largely located in territory controlled by ethnic armed groups fighting the military, while China, the main buyer of Myanmar rare earths, could balk at any US role.

The US last week lifted sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the country's military, saying the move was part of a new approach to the country.

"This approach highlights the importance of pursuing dialogue with all groups involved in Burma’s civil war and commits to re-examining the range of tools the United States has historically leveraged to promote core interests in the country," the State Department said of the sanctions move.

Min Aung Hlaing remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses, including for his role in the coup and crushing a subsequent popular uprising, and the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims that Washington declared a genocide. The armed forces have killed thousands of people in airstrikes since the putsch, which sparked widespread civil war, the United Nations says.

The latest engagements in Japan show the Trump administration views Myanmar through a "purely transactionalist lens," said Hunter Marston, Southeast Asia director at the Lowy Institute, an Australian think tank.

"The critical minerals and rare earths that Myanmar holds are viewed as probably the chief strategic asset that Washington is interested in within Myanmar," Marston said.

JAPAN'S ROLE UNCLEAR

It is unclear whether Japan has any stake in the US-Myanmar talks beyond playing host, including for earlier talks in the Japanese capital in June, but there are signs that Tokyo is also moving to re-engage with Myanmar.

Japan's acting envoy to Myanmar met with the foreign minister of Myanmar's military-backed government earlier this month in their first known public engagement. Tokyo does not formally recognise the administration.

That meeting followed a September visit by Japanese ruling party lawmaker Hiromichi Watanabe to Naypyitaw, which he said was aimed at restarting bilateral cooperation and resuming development aid to Myanmar, according to the state-run Global New Light of Myanmar newspaper.

Japan's Foreign Ministry said the acting envoy raised issues such as protection for Japanese nationals and support for Japanese companies, while Watanabe's trip was in his capacity as an individual member of parliament and "does not in any way prejudge" the position of the government.

Watanabe told Reuters his trip was aimed at preparing the environment to normalise relations, though he acknowledged that barriers remained.

Japan condemned the military's 2021 overthrow of Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government but stopped short of joining the US and other Western governments in imposing sanctions on junta leaders and military-linked entities.

Tokyo was one of Myanmar's largest foreign investors, seeking to counter China's influence in one of Asia's last frontier markets. Unlike numerous Western firms, many Japanese companies remained despite the turmoil that followed the 2021 coup.

Around 300 Japanese companies still operate in Myanmar, down from more than 400 in 2020, according to Japan's trade promotion agency, JETRO.

data.title: Stocktwits Weekly Spread: What Shaped Treasury Yields And The Dollar This Week
data.description:
Key points:
  • The U.S. dollar index dropped 0.2% on Friday, completing its sharpest weekly decline since early September as traders lowered probabilities of an October rate hike to 20%.
  • The U.S. Treasury Department released primary dealer survey questions that omitted direct references to cutting 20-year bond issuances or scaling back long-end debt auctions. 
  • The yield curve flattened further this week, with 10-year yields falling about 16 basis points over the previous week.

U.S. government bond prices retreated, and the dollar suffered its sharpest weekly decline in over a month during the week ending Oct. 16, as fixed-income investors digested ambiguous signals from Kevin Warsh on the future course of interest rates.

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh declined to provide forward guidance on interest rate trajectory during remarks at the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok. Warsh's silence led traders to pare back probabilities of an October rate hike to 20%.

"Warsh offered no guidance, which while it should be expected of him at this point, the market is taking it as a signal that the October Fed meeting is likely a no go," Noah Buffam at CIVB Capital Markets told Bloomberg in an interview.

Moreover, adding to the dissent among fixed income traders, the U.S. Department of the Treasury did not provide information or explicit proposals to reduce long-duration debt issuances or eliminate 20-year auctions, which primary dealers were expecting.

The 30-year U.S. Treasury yield slipped 17 basis points from the previous week to 5.43%, while the 10-year yield eased slightly to 5.08% and 2-year yields settled at 4.72% for the week ending Oct. 16.

The spread between the U.S. 10-year yield and the U.S. 2-year yield ticked lower to 0.37% in the week, from 0.44% a week ago.

The iShares 20+ Year Treasury ETF (TLT) ended the week 2.7% higher, while the shorter-duration iShares 1-3 year ETF (SHY) added about 0.2%. The slight recovery in the shorter-duration bond ETF may reflect easing short-term inflation pressure; however, markets still factor in one more rate hike in December.

Retail sentiment on TLT and SHY was ‘bullish,’ with ‘high’ message volumes.

The Dollar Spot Index slipped 0.2% on Friday, snapping a multi-week rally and registering its worst weekly performance since September 4. The dollar fell against all major developed market currencies, allowing the euro to break a five-week losing streak.

data.title: Stocktwits Fintech Pulse: US Fintech Weekly Briefing & Market Drivers
data.description:
Key points:
  • PayPal extended its rally on AI-driven shopping expansion, while Fiserv faced price target cuts over its revenue growth projections.
  • SoFi Technologies and Affirm Holdings (AFRM) continue to navigate interest rate headwinds, ending the week lower.
  • The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) launched a formal enforcement initiative targeting unlawful "debanking" practices by major financial institutions. 

Regulatory measures by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) to tackle unlawful debanking practices by financial institutions, a range of analyst price target and outlook shifts, and tech market volatility affecting payment processors and retail brokerages were central themes during the week of October 12.

Fintechs with yield-bearing deposit products continued to tackle pressure from the Federal Reserve's recent interest rate hike along with increasing bets for another bump in rates at the end of the year. While elevated interest rates help net interest margins for deposit-heavy platforms, they temper consumer borrowing appetite, which has already taken a hit on account of soaring inflationary pressures.

Infrastructure Shifts Across Mastercard, PayPal, And Fiserv 

Mastercard Incorporated (MA): Mastercard announced a strategic partnership on Oct. 12 with WEX to launch the Asia-Pacific region’s first unified fleet payments network, integrating fuel, maintenance, and tolling transactions into a single infrastructure.

PayPal Holdings Inc. (PYPL): PayPal shares extended a multi-day rally, ending its second consecutive week higher, after the company announced partnering with AI shopping agent provider Glance to embed instant AI-driven shopping checkout capabilities.

Fiserv Inc. (FISV): Cantor Fitzgerald, Barclays, and TD Cowen lowered their price targets amid an ongoing shareholder lawsuit that urged a federal court to deny Fiserv's motion on the back of revenue guidance resets. However, despite the price target cuts, FISV stock ended the week about 4% higher.

How Neobank SoFi Performed 

SoFi Technologies Inc. (SOFI): SoFi shares dropped to a 52-week low of $13.86 amid investor concerns over revenue expansion outpacing bottom-line profitability gains.

While the platform posted Q2 net revenue of $1.22 billion and bumped its full-year top-line guidance to a range of $4.75 billion to $4.85 billion, full-year adjusted EPS projections held flat near $0.60 as elevated marketing spend and acquisition expenses squeezed profit margins.

Last week, Keefe Bruyette lowered its price target for SoFi to $15 from $16 and maintained an ‘Underperform’ rating. The firm expects rising interest rates and SoFi’s growing balance sheet to create more than $1 billion in pressure this quarter, forcing the company to issue more loans while reducing its available capital.

Analysts Bearish On Robinhood 

Wells Fargo lowered Robinhood's price target to $120 from $125 and kept an Equal Weight rating on the shares earlier this week. Meanwhile, founder and CEO Vlad Tenev sold nearly $43 million in company stock this month, but Barron's reported he’s far from cashing out.

Tenev’s stock sale aligned with a broader surge in Bitcoin in early October, which propelled the digital asset above $86,000. However, this upward trajectory hit friction as digital currency markets encountered macroeconomic headwinds from surging crude prices and advancing Treasury yields.

Robinhood share price dropped over 9% this week to record its fourth consecutive weekly decline.

Federal Rules And Legal Updates 

On Oct. 14, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau announced a targeted initiative investigating major financial institutions for potential unlawful "debanking". The investigation evaluates whether arbitrary account closures violate the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) or rules prohibiting unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices (UDAAP).

data.title: Stocktwits Zero To Sixty — Tesla’s Roadster Flies With SpaceX Thrusters, Rivian Opens Cars To AI Agents, And Lucid Eyes France
data.description:
Key points:
  • Tesla showed the redesigned Roadster at a SpaceX site near Waco, claiming sub-1-second 0-60 mph, more than 230 mph top speed, and 2028 production, with reservations starting at $50,000.
  • Rivian said future vehicles will run third-party AI agents and received EPA approval for longer-range 2027 commercial vans with a 129 kWh pack.
  • GM’s Mary Barra defended the exit from Cruise robotaxis while staying on track for eyes-off driving by 2028.

Electric vehicles outpaced consumer imagination this week after giant Tesla Inc (TSLA) finally unveiled its long-delayed next-generation Roadster on Thursday with SpaceX thrusters that let the car drive upside down, flip midair, and jump obstacles as high as the company’s own Semi truck, while rivals stuck to advancing software, commercial products, and markets.

Tesla Roadster Takes Flight

Tesla on Thursday unveiled the redesigned Roadster at a SpaceX test site near Waco in Texas. The vehicle is developed with technology borrowed from SpaceX, and the display model showed a two-seater interior with a suction system that Musk assured will ease corner maneuvering in addition to helping the car hang upside down, and cold gas thrusters that allow it to flip in the air.

Vehicle engineering chief Lars Moravy said the car can accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in less than one second and reach a top speed of more than 230 mph, with range listed above 300 miles. Musk at the event also termed the car potentially “the only manually driven car Tesla makes,” though stunts at the event were performed autonomously. He also said that the vehicle might not be legal in all jurisdictions.

Production for the vehicle, which Musk has previously warned will not move the needle for Tesla financials in a big way, is slated to start in 2028. The company did not disclose a price point for the vehicle, but updated its reservation page to list three variants, including a base version one can reserve for $50,000, a Thrust model which can be reserved for $250,000, and a limited edition Rocket single-seat variant which is invite-only. Tesla said in its reservation agreement that it cannot confirm the purchase price of the vehicle just yet, and reservation holders will know the cost only once they have configured their vehicle order at a later date.

Rivian Pushes AI Agents And Longer-Range Vans

Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe said at TechCrunch Disrupt this week that future Rivian vehicles will be able to run AI agents from outside companies such as Anthropic, building on the company’s own in-car assistant. He described an agentic framework that routes voice requests to local or cloud models depending on complexity. Timing was not given; the company instead pointed to its December AI & Autonomy Day.

Separately, Rivian received EPA approval for 2027 model-year commercial vans with a larger 129 kWh LFP battery and optional dual-motor all-wheel drive. The larger pack raises the EDV 700's lab-tested range to 355 miles in front-wheel-drive and 322 miles with all-wheel drive, Electric Vehicles reported.

Lucid Eyes New Market

Lucid, meanwhile, announced plans to deliver its electric vehicles in France starting in the first quarter of 2027 as it tackles weak demand for its higher-end offerings.

The company intends to open its initial retail and service locations in France, working with local partner Emil Frey France, and aims to expand the network to more than 16 partner sites by the end of the year. Vehicles are on display this week at the Paris Motor Show, running October 12–18, marking Lucid’s first appearance at the event.

Ford-Geely JV Clears

Chinese regulators unconditionally approved a joint venture between Ford and Geely that lets Geely take a portion of Ford’s dormant Valencia plant in Spain for local production aimed at avoiding tariffs. The partners also plan a Blue Oval-badged SUV on Geely’s platform expected to be offered with more than one powertrain type, and production targeted for 2028.

General Motors’ Barra Defends Exit From Robotaxis

General Motors CEO Mary Barra, speaking on CNBC’s Mad Money this week, reaffirmed that the company remains on track for eyes-off, hands-off driving in personal vehicles by 2028, starting with the electric Cadillac Escalade IQ. She defended the decision to exit the all-electric Cruise robotaxi business after spending more than $10 billion, saying GM is “not in the taxi business” or “the bus business” even while rivals attempt to scale autonomous vehicles.

GM exited Cruise in late 2024 and folded the unit into its driver-assistance efforts after one of its electric robotaxis was involved in an accident in San Francisco. “When we looked at the capital that we were going to need… It was a tough decision, but I think it was the right decision,” she said.

How Did Retail Traders React?

On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around TSLA and F stayed within the bearish territory over the past 24 hours, while sentiment around RIVN and GM stayed within the neutral territory. Sentiment around LCID was bullish at the time of writing.

TSLA has dropped 21% year-to-date. GM and F have clocked single-digit gains or losses in the period, while LCID slipped 70% and RIVN dropped 34%.

data.title: Brent crude hits $110 for first time since May; U.S. WTI tops $100
data.description:
Brent crude oil hit $110/bbl for the first time since May, and WTI crude rose by the largest weekly percentage since July on concerns over continued Middle East supply risks and uncertainty over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, as well as Ukraine's renewed targeting of Russian refineries.

Shipping risks remain high after two cargo ships sank near the Strait of Hormuz following attacks this week, and risks to shipping have raised freight and insurance costs, contributing to the higher price of oil.

Ukraine reportedly struck Russia's Ryazan ⁠refinery on Thursday after President Zelenskyy declared his country was abandoning a ceasefire covering energy sites announced a week ago by President Trump.

"We're still in a bull market," BOK Financial senior VP of trading Dennis Kissler said in a note, as flows through the Strait of Hormuz are not reliable, expectations of Russian diesel coming onto the market are not being met, and with Ukrainian attacks on refineries, "those barrels are going to have trouble getting to the market."

A third factor is that demand destruction "at least in the U.S. is not happening," Kissler added, noting this week's report of surprisingly large drawdowns of U.S. fuel inventories, with distillate inventories—which include diesel and heating oil—at 102.6M barrels, according to the Energy Information Administration, down 12% Y/Y.

The U.S. Department of Energy requested an exchange of up to 17M ​barrels of crude from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve on Friday, after previously agreeing to loan 172M barrels of oil from the SPR as part of a wider deal with International Energy Agency member states to release 400M barrels from reserves around the world.

However, oil prices above $100 look increasingly stretched relative to market fundamentals, as Middle Eastern exports have largely recovered and global oil inventories remain comfortable, Julius Baer's Norbert Rucker said in a note.

Diesel supply concerns could also ease as higher product exports and reduced refinery maintenance support availability, Rucker added.

On Friday, front-month Nymex crude for November delivery jumped 3.5% to $101.41, its highest settlement value since September 17, and front-month Brent crude for December delivery surged 3.7% to $109.86/bbl, its best close since May 19.

Front-month Nymex ULSD (HO1:COM) for November delivery added 1.1% on Friday to $4.8991/gal, while front-month Nymex RBOB November gasoline (XB1:COM) gained 1.7% to $3.2354/gal.

For the full week, Nymex soared 10.4%, its largest one-week percentage gain since the week ending July 17, Brent crude climbed 4.9%, its fourth consecutive weekly gain, ULSD jumped 3.4%, but RBOB fell 1.8%.

U.S. natural gas futures fell on Friday as the market appeared to look past this weekend's anticipated cold spell in the Northeast that is expected to drive up residential and commercial heating demand; the front-month Nymex November contract fell 3.7% on Friday to $3.1160/MMBtu, down 3.2% on the week.

Friday's top five stocks on the S&P 500 leaderboard belonged to the oil and gas sector: Targa Resources up 4.4%, Diamondback Energy up 4.3%, EOG Resources up 4.2%, Kinder Morgan up 4.2%, APA Corp. up 4.1%.

data.title: The Power Watch Is the New Power Move for Women at Work — WSJ
data.description:
By Tara Weiss

Julianna Wanner, a partner manager in advertising sales, was trying to win over a prospective client at dinner last October when she noticed the Rolex on his wrist. "Cool Datejust," she said.

The remark prompted a wide-ranging conversation about their shared passion for watches. Exchanging stories, he told her that he bought the timepiece to commemorate reaching $1 million in revenue for the business he built. She landed the client, and the deal helped her exceed her quarterly revenue goal. She credits the watch talk with helping build the rapport that closed the deal.

Wanner, 31, is among a growing number of women who say that becoming a watch enthusiast has become an unexpected workplace advantage, giving them an entree into conversations traditionally dominated by men. Watches are a hobby worn on the wrist, making enthusiasts easy to spot. A comment about a timepiece can open the door to stories about a milestone purchase, a family heirloom or a passion for collecting.

"It's a male-dominated hobby," said Wanner, who lives in Los Angeles. "When a woman says 'I love your [Omega] Speedmaster,' it raises eyebrows."

Last year, she marked her 30th birthday and career milestones with a large Cartier Tank Française, automatic movement, which cost $6,750.

Entry-level luxury watches can go for a couple thousand dollars, while the most coveted models can cost upward of $60,000 and be hard to get, with long wait lists at some dealers.

"It establishes social status, peer-to-peer status and signals that I'm not a tiny woman in the back who doesn't know how I got into the room," said Nicole Cost, an executive at Bank of America in Greenwich, Conn., who works with high-net-worth individuals on trusts and estate planning. "It builds trust."

Cost became interested in watch collecting while attending watch events with her husband, where she found herself drawn to vintage pieces. She wears three watches in rotation: a $7,500 Hermès H08 in brushed titanium; a Rolex Datejust with blue Roman numeral dial from 1984, which she said cost about $6,000; and a Rolex Oysterdate Precision from the 1950s, which she said cost about $4,750.

She once noticed one of her clients wearing a Breitling Emergency, a $17,650 to $22,400 technical watch with a built-in locator that can transmit distress signals for search-and-rescue teams. Knowing it's often worn by skiers, she used it as an opening to talk to him about the sport.

Cost said that she's still one of few women at watch events. But women's interest in watches has risen in recent years.

Sales of women's watches in the U.S. have more than doubled in the last three years and more than quadrupled in the last six on Chrono24, a global luxury-watch marketplace, according to company spokesman Johannes Förster. Cartier has the highest share of women's-watch spending on the site, he said, and that share continues to grow.

Dimepiece, an online media platform dedicated to women who love watches, launched in 2020 and now has around 62,000 followers on Instagram and around 1,200 subscribers on Substack. Its founder, Brynn Wallner, said she had discovered "watches are cool" working at her previous job in editorial at Sotheby's.

"I was about to turn 30 and felt like the watch industry missed me as a consumer," she said. "Why aren't there websites or Instagram [accounts] for me?" Her site offers information for first-time buyers and seasoned collectors as well as celebrity watch sightings and interviews with influencers about their first watch.

These women are already in the rooms they've historically been left out of. Now, their watch hobby is helping them build connections and be taken more seriously, said Laurie Henneborn, vice president of research, insights and solutions at Catalyst, an organization that studies women at work.

"That's about much more than watches," she said. "It's about social capital and who gets access."

Erica Eckes, 29, a director of strategy at a tech company living in Charlotte, N.C., bought her "gateway drug," a $6,795 Cartier Panthère, to celebrate a promotion. When she later became a director, she purchased a Rolex Datejust model that retails for $18,000.

At a dinner with her leadership team in a previous job, she noticed her boss's boss — the company's new chief revenue officer — wearing a Breitling Navitimer, which can go for as much as $54,000 for solid gold or limited-edition variants. He told her the timepiece was a gift from his wife and kids, and they compared notes on watches and the stories behind their collections.

For her next watch, Eckes is torn between an A. Lange & Söhne 1815 Up/Down, priced at about $40,000, or a vintage Piaget stone-dial dress-watch, which costs from $5,000 to $30,000.

She's turning 30 soon, a milestone birthday. "There's potential for either scenario," she said.

data.title: The Most Polite Trucker in America Is a Driverless 18-Wheeler — WSJ
data.description:
By Esther Fung | Photography and Video by Drew Ducote for WSJ

On a busy freight corridor, the 240 miles of I-45 between Dallas and Houston, it was bumper-to-bumper, like usual, when something out-of-the-ordinary happened. A big rig let in several cars from the on-ramp. Another 18-wheeler changed lanes to make space for a truck pulled over on the shoulder.

Neither honked its horn — the baritone blasts anyone who has ever driven a hatchback can't forget.

They're driverless trucks: they don't need to honk and can't on their own, said Aurora Innovation, a major driverless trucker. The trucks have a perception system that adjusts quickly without having to slam the brakes and sees and avoids potential hazards early. And without a driver, no honking in annoyance.

"It's our job to continue to operate safely and build trust," said Chris Urmson, who was the chief technology officer of Google's self-driving car project that became Waymo and is now CEO of Aurora.

Self-driving cars are on the cusp of moving from novelty to commonplace. Waymo driverless taxis buzz around cities like San Francisco and Phoenix. Next up are the biggest, loudest, most-daunting-to-other-drivers vehicles on the highway: the trucks.

As more goods are trucked across the U.S. every day, moving them is getting more expensive. Businesses complain of an acute driver shortage. Drivers need to stop after 11 hours to rest; driverless trucks don't, saving both time and fuel. The cost of diesel has risen 62% since late February.

This stretch of Texas, flat, straight and filled with trucks, is the perfect testing spot for dozens of driverless big rigs, some without a human driver and others with one riding along just in case. About half a dozen companies, including Aurora, develop the technology for driverless trucks and team up with truck makers to produce them. Aurora, based in Pittsburgh, expects to have 200 autonomous trucks on highways in Texas and nearby states by year-end, up from around 30 big rigs today.

Volvo Autonomous Solutions said it plans to roll out 300 autonomous trucks with Aurora and Waabi, another autonomous-trucking company, by the end of 2027 that would run in Texas and Oklahoma. Aurora estimates that by 2030, 30,000 autonomous trucks could be on the roads.

"I have never seen a more supportive regulatory environment from the federal government," said Lior Ron, chief operating officer of Waabi. That includes removing obstacles to the commercial deployment of trucks, he added.

Without a federal safety standard specifically governing autonomous trucks, states are coming up with their own frameworks for the trucks. Around two dozen states, mostly in the southern half of the U.S., now allow autonomous trucks on the road without a human operator under certain conditions.

Technology companies have promised autonomous big rigs for years but ran into technological, funding and other hurdles. This time, the companies say they have completed hundreds of thousands of miles of testing.

Amazon, Walmart, PepsiCo and IKEA have carried out pilot runs with autonomous trucks in recent years. Some tested smaller box trucks. Others tried the biggest commercial trucks that weigh up to 80,000 pounds when fully loaded. A midsize sedan, by comparison, is roughly 3,500 pounds.

In the Permian Basin in West Texas, several driverless trucks have been pounding the dusty roads transporting frack sand to well sites.

"Its ability to see long distances is better than a human driver," said Matt Detmar, chief executive of Detmar Logistics, which currently uses two driverless Aurora trucks to transport sand in a 60-mile loop in Midland, Texas. The trucks use lidar to see more clearly in the dark, dust and foggy weather and can react faster or avoid a hazard.

There have been 69 reported fatal crashes linked to an automated-driving system or an advanced driver assistance system from July 2021 to August 2026, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. None of these fatal crashes involved a truck equipped with an automated-driving system, NHTSA says.

On I-45, IKEA plans to use a Kodiak AI driverless truck by the end of the year to ship its furniture 219 miles, part of the delivery route connecting its distribution center in Baytown, Texas, with its Frisco store. Human drivers will cover the first and final-mile portions. IKEA has done test runs in Kodiak's truck for four years, completing over 1,300 deliveries.

"We see significant potential, particularly for long-haul transport. The logistics industry faces long-term challenges related to driver availability, increasing demand for freight movement and the need for greater efficiency, predictability and resilience," said IKEA spokesman Oscar Ljunggren.

Trucks often go along repeatable routes, which is more convenient for going driverless. The driverless tractor-trailers rely on several cameras and sensors mounted at the front and sides that include radar and lidar equipment to help determine what's on the road. Inside the cab or the tractor, there remains a steering wheel and seats.

Today, a typical driverless truck run is best suited for what shippers call the middle-mile, or the stretch from depot to depot. It looks like this: Humans load a trailer and drive it to a depot where they hand it off to a driverless tractor. Without a human, the truck drives from depot to another depot or yard where the trailer is either unloaded or a human driver takes over for docking or driving the final mile. Driverless 18-wheelers can't back up without a human driver, though the companies say they're working on adding that feature.

"We believe in the strategy of using it in the middle mile," said Eric Hildenbrand, chief legal, strategy and administrative officer at McLane, one of the largest distributors to convenience stores and chain restaurants in the country.

McLane has a fleet of 3,700 tractors and 5,900 trailers, and aims to add up to 10 Aurora trucks by year-end. It employs more than 6,000 drivers and wants its employees to be at the final mile when they unload and wheel their freight into restaurants or stores like 7-Eleven.

Current regulations limit long-haul drivers to a maximum of driving for 11 hours within a single 14-hour on-duty window, followed by a mandatory 10-hour break. A truck driver driving from Dallas to Atlanta would have to stop somewhere along the 780-mile journey to rest. Driverless trucks don't.

They use diesel and have to refuel. The driverless-trucking companies arrange for attendants at a gas station to fill them up.

It cost an average of $2.34 per mile to operate a truck in 2025, and about 44% of that represents driver wages and benefits, according to the American Transportation Research Institute. Fuel made up 21% of the cost in 2025. Autonomous trucks can reduce fuel consumption by 10% because they can calibrate speeds and optimize acceleration, braking and coasting with more precision, the companies say. Goldman Sachs forecasts that autonomous trucking will become cost-competitive with human-operated trucks in 2028 in the U.S.

In tests, many driverless trucks have what the industry calls "a safety driver" riding in the cab who can take over if there are emergencies or glitches. Jorge Baeza, retired as a truck driver and has worked for Kodiak since 2021.

Early on, the braking mechanism was harsh and the trucks sometimes unexpectedly stopped when approaching an overpass. Baeza, who was a Kodiak safety driver, used to ask supervisors, "Can I take over?" "Now, it's so much smoother," he says. Now, as Kodiak assisted autonomy operator, he can remotely honk the horn of an autonomous truck on the road, if needed, from the command center.

Sounding alarms about driverless trucks are some drivers' associations.

The International Brotherhood of Teamsters in California filed a lawsuit in August against the state's Department of Motor Vehicles opposing new state regulations that removed a ban on driverless trucks weighing 10,001 pounds or more, and allowed testing and deployment of such vehicles through a permit process.

"The deployment of Self-Driving Trucks, authorized by the regulatory changes, has the potential to eventually wipe out the jobs of more than 200,000 employee semi-truck drivers working across California," the complaint said.

Peter Finn, who serves as the Teamsters' vice president at-large, said that truck driving is the most common job for men without a college degree in the country. He added that communities want to see investments in people and middle-class jobs against the broader backdrop of artificial-intelligence growth.

The Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association opposes a new Transportation Department ruling that some autonomous truck companies may use cab-mounted warning beacons instead of placing a reflective triangle on the road when a truck stops on the highway. The DOT had previously denied the exemption request by Aurora and Waymo in December 2024.

"This corporate carve-out sets a troubling precedent," said Todd Spencer, president and CEO of the OOIDA.

In the Permian Basin in West Texas, on any given day, 500 to 600 trucks are deployed delivering frack sand for Detmar Logistics, which operates 24 hours-a-day, 365 days a year. Drivers typically work three weeks and then take a week off, meaning a truck is only in operation 75% of the time. After factoring rest rules that include hours-of-service limits, typically 11 or 12 hours, the utilization rate of the truck falls to 40%.

Detmar has about 180 drivers on payroll, who each make about $80,000 to $120,000 a year. Detmar said he isn't planning to reduce his workforce. Instead, with more autonomous trucks in the fleet, he hopes to offer them a more predictable work schedule.

Detmar has been using two Aurora driverless trucks seven days a week, 20 hours a day and expects to add about 30 autonomous trucks from Aurora by the end of the year.

data.title: Blue Owl Founders Promised a Comeback. The Company's Share Price Hasn't Budged. — WSJ
data.description:
By Matt Wirz

When Blue Owl found itself at the center of the backlash against private credit in early March, its top executives sought to calm staff, telling them in a firmwide meeting, "We're going to emerge stronger from this storm."

Not so far.

Blue Owl stock is still stuck, down about 67% from its record high in January 2025. Prices recently dipped to near all-time lows, a gut punch for the many employees who get much of their pay in shares.

The company disclosed this month that clients asked to withdraw 17% of their money from its largest private-credit fund in the most recent quarter, more than the redemption requests most competitors received. A smaller fund that Blue Owl tried to restructure last year recently reported its worst loss since the height of the Covid pandemic.

Co-founders Doug Ostrover and Marc Lipschultz built Blue Owl into a star of the private-credit industry, a parallel banking system with loans stretching across the U.S. economy. Some current and former employees now say the firm relied too much on wealthy individuals for growth and has struggled to respond to the private-credit backlash effectively.

In the March meeting, Ostrover told staff the issues the firm faces stemmed from "vicious" media coverage and envious rivals who were "always kind of on the prowl," according to a recording of the previously unreported meeting obtained by The Wall Street Journal.

"You should remember you only get attention as a company if you matter," Ostrover said.

Investment bankers have been circling the company, meeting with its founders to propose a full or partial sale of the business, according to people familiar with the matter.

"The real test of a business is how it performs under pressure," Ostrover said in a response to a request for comment. "We've built a diversified firm with multiple investment platforms, numerous sources of capital and a long-term approach to investing."

Blue Owl executives have been trying to recast the company, growing areas outside of private credit and promoting funds sold to institutions such as pensions and insurers. Fundraising from institutional investors rose to 66% of overall inflows in the past 12 months, Lipschultz said in a July presentation to Wall Street analysts.

But overall, fundraising is down. Fundraising from institutional investors declined 22% in the second quarter compared with the same period last year and only grew as a proportion of Blue Owl's total sales because flows from individual investors slumped even more, dropping about 60%, the company's financial statements show.

"The long-term trend is one of strong growth and continued institutional demand for our platform," Blue Owl's spokesman said.

For future growth, Ostrover and Lipschultz have placed a huge wager on financing and building AI data centers. Strong fundraising in that business could offset problems in private credit but there is also risk of a backlash against artificial intelligence, analysts say. Ostrover wants to build fundraising from insurers, a strategy that some competitors have been building for years.

Blue Owl's chief executives teamed up to launch the company in 2016 after neither one got the top job at their prior firms, Blackstone for Ostrover and KKR for Lipschultz. The duo reached over $300 billion in assets under management by marketing "retail" funds to wealthy individuals and acquiring at least eight companies, starting in 2021 with Dyal, a fund-manager stakes business.

Ostrover realized early that individual investors were crucial because they offered more growth potential than pensions and other institutions, which had invested for years in private credit. "We often refer to this as our hidden gem," he said about the retail-fund business during a 2020 presentation.

The firm amassed about $50 billion from individuals from 2022 to 2025, streaking past jealous competitors. Companies Blue Owl lends to include BMC Software, the PetVet Care Centers chain and Bazooka Candy.

Costs from hiring, junkets and pro-sport endorsements to build the retail operation added up and drew ire from other divisions, the current and former employees said. When spending cuts were instituted in summer of 2025 — as business was still booming — executives in other parts of the business blamed the private-wealth division.

The firm implemented "expense-management policies," not firmwide cuts, the company spokesman said.

Last fall, Blue Owl's gem turned into kryptonite as droves of individual investors tried to pull money out of private-credit funds amid a spate of defaults and mounting worries that loans made to software companies would go bad. The firm caused further panic in February when it announced plans to partially cash out investors in the fund it had tried to restructure by selling $600 million of loans it held.

The plan gave clients about 30% of their money back. It also drew questions from stock analysts about why Blue Owl didn't immediately disclose what investments would be left in the fund or that one of the four buyers it sold loans to was a related insurance company, Kuvare.

By August, the fund had returned an additional 13% of clients' money as it sold more loans and others got paid back, which boosted the percentage of problem loans in the remaining portfolio. Blue Owl disclosed in August that roughly 10% of the loans still in the fund were in default and another 20% were underperforming.

Selling loans to fund client payouts delivered "a result for the investors that is far beyond what any other equivalent product has accomplished," the Blue Owl spokesman said. The firm's larger and newer funds have lower than average default rates.

Meanwhile, employees have been jolted by sharp drops in the value of stock-based pay that could take years to recover. Many senior staff receive roughly half of their annual compensation in deferred stock. Transplants from the companies Blue Owl bought also expected big payouts in now-devalued shares.

Some employees are heading for the exit. A managing director in Blue Owl's Tokyo office defected to Benefit Street Partners, while a managing director in institutional funds went to Pimco and a principal in the private-wealth unit took a job at KKR.

About 5.6% of Blue Owl employees have quit annually over the past three years, below the alternative fund management industry average, the company spokesman said. The firm recently hired a head of institutional capital in Japan, a managing director in real estate and a head of insurance.

Ostrover held the all-hands meeting in March after being flooded with questions from concerned employees. Mistakes had been made, especially in public relations, he told them. "We need to learn and improve. We did not do everything perfectly," he said.

Finance chief Alan Kirshenbaum followed Ostrover's remarks with a slideshow. The slide deck didn't detail a crisis response. Instead it showed how the stock price of KKR, one of Blue Owl's larger competitors, plunged 38% in 2015 as energy investments soured. Kirshenbaum blamed the decline on negative headlines. "We unfortunately know how that feels," he said, before pointing out that KKR stock has since soared.

data.title: Stocktwits Biotech Dealmaker: Gilead, AstraZeneca And Roche Chase Pipeline Expansion Over Buyouts
data.description:
Key points:
  • Gilead Sciences partnered with Vir Biotechnology on Wednesday to discover and develop three drugs aimed at solid tumors.
  • AstraZeneca signed an up-to-$1.5 billion AI collaboration with insitro for MASH and cardiomyopathies. 
  • Roche licensed Rona’s drug candidate, and Zealand Pharma teamed with Generate on AI-designed proteins for differentiated obesity approaches.

Large pharmaceutical companies including Gilead Sciences, Roche and AstraZeneca spent this week securing access to discovery technologies and experimental candidates that address clear biological gaps, instead of large-scale acquisitions of rival firms or approved products.

Obesity and cancer remained the clear focal points, with several of the week’s biggest partnerships aimed at differentiated weight-loss mechanisms or new solid-tumor approaches.

Gilead Partners With Vir For New Cancer Drug Candidates

Gilead Sciences (GILD) partnered with Vir Biotechnology (VIR) on Wednesday to discover and develop three drugs aimed at solid tumors. Vir will handle early discovery, design, and optimization using its AI-enabled protein engineering tools and PRO-XTEN masking technology. Gilead receives exclusive rights to nominate candidates and will lead subsequent development, manufacturing, and commercialization.

Vir is eligible for $90 million upfront—$65 million in cash plus a $25 million equity investment at a premium—plus up to $45 million in near-term preclinical milestones and as much as $1.74 billion in later development, regulatory, and commercial payments, along with tiered royalties. The agreement marks Vir’s second major partnership around its masking platform this year after a previous deal with Astellas and adds to Gilead’s attempts to advance its cancer offerings besides its blockbuster drug Trodelvy.

AstraZeneca Taps Insitro’s AI Platform

AstraZeneca (AZN) signed a worldwide exclusive research collaboration with privately held AI therapeutics company insitro focused on metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and cardiomyopathies. Insitro will apply its Virtual Human platform, which combines human and cellular data with AI, to identify causal disease biology and advance AstraZeneca-nominated targets through discovery to the development-candidate stage.

AstraZeneca will lead clinical development, regulatory work, and commercialization. Insitro will receive $40 million upfront and is eligible for up to approximately $1.46 billion in discovery, development, and commercial milestones, plus single-digit royalties on potential sales.

Roche, Zealand Pharma Add Differentiated Obesity Approaches

Roche secured exclusive worldwide rights to Rona Therapeutics’ investigational drug candidate which targets a protein predominantly expressed in fat tissues. The drug candidate is designed to selectively reduce visceral and ectopic fat while preserving lean mass—an attractive complement to currently popular obesity drug classes like GLP-1. Rona is eligible for up to $100 million in upfront and near-term payments, up to $1.06 billion in additional milestones, and tiered royalties.

Separately, Zealand Pharma entered a collaboration with Generate Biomedicines (GENB) to design multispecific protein therapeutics for obesity and other metabolic diseases using Generate’s generative AI platform. Generate will lead research through lead-candidate selection for two initial programs, with an option for a third; Zealand will handle clinical development, regulatory submissions, and commercialization. Generate receives $30 million upfront, up to $35 million in early preclinical milestones, and nearly $1.2 billion in total potential milestones, plus royalties.

Pfizer, Galderma Make Platform And Commercial Moves

Pfizer (PFE) partnered with privately-held Enodia Therapeutics on a research collaboration and license for compounds intended to block disease-driving proteins at the point of synthesis. The potential value exceeds $500 million, including an upfront payment, milestones, and royalties; Enodia will run discovery against multiple targets while Pfizer takes over later development and commercialization.

XBI has fallen 4% over the past week as part of a broader biotech pullback that began after its mid-August peak near $170, but it is up 22.5% year-to-date.

data.title: Trump mocks popularity of the name Mohammad, common among Muslims
data.description:
By Steve Holland and Kanishka Singh

US President Donald Trump made a joke about the popularity of the name Mohammad in the Muslim world as he mocked Iran's presidency during a campaign speech on Friday.

"You know, if you're in doubt about somebody's name from the Middle East, just say 'Mohammad,'" Trump told a crowd in Dalton, Georgia. "You have about a 65% chance. 'Hello, Mohammad.' I've done it for years now. I've never been wrong."

Mohammad is one of the most common male names among Muslims, who often name their sons after the Prophet Mohammad, the founder of Islam.

Trump made the comment as he was discussing Iran during a rally in a hangar at Dalton Municipal Airport in Georgia, where he campaigned for Republican political candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

"Iran is the only country where nobody wants to be president," Trump said, then pretended to ask several people named Mohammad whether they wanted the job. Masoud Pezeshkian has been president of Iran since 2024.

The Georgia crowd gave the joke a muted response.

Rights advocates and Muslim advocacy groups have repeatedly criticized Trump for rhetoric that they say demonizes and mocks Muslims, immigrants and ethnic minorities.

He has escalated such rhetoric during the midterm campaign season, particularly against Somali and Muslim Americans including Muslim Democratic ‌US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Representative Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat who came to the US as a Somali refugee.

Trump repeated his vow that Iran would never get a nuclear weapon, seven months after the United States and Israel launched a war on Tehran aimed in part at crippling its nuclear program.

An annual report by the Council on American Islamic Relations released earlier this year attributed rising Islamophobia in the US in part to Trump's crackdown on immigration and pro-Palestinian protests during his second term.

data.description:
By Andrew Bary

Berkshire Hathaway is famous for its value orientation. So why is it betting on Bending Spoons, a quirky and richly priced technology conglomerate? This past week, Berkshire added $330 million in stock on top of the $600 million investment it made in Bending Spoons' initial public offering in July.

Bending Spoons, based in Milan, has assembled a group of technology castoffs, such as AOL and Brightcove. Its unusual name, a nod to psychic powers, comes from the sci-fi classic The Matrix. Its stock is anything but cheap, trading for about 10 times forward sales and more than 30 times estimated 2027 earnings, well above the S&P 500's valuation.

So what has attracted Berkshire, the Warren Buffett creation, to Bending Spoons? A new direction under newish CEO Greg Abel? Berkshire won't say. Berkshire has made tech investments, notably Apple, but it generally won't pay a premium price.

Henry Ellenbogen, founder of Durable Capital Partners, spelled out some of the company's charms at the Barron's July Midyear Roundtable: "We believe Bending Spoons' revenue and Ebitda per employee will continue to compound, allowing the company to drive better organic growth and strong operating leverage."

So far, the move is a big win for both Berkshire and Bending Spoons. The latter's stock jumped 45% in the past week and Berkshire has a paper profit of about $800 million so far.

With inflation up 3.7%, the possibility of the Federal Reserve hiking interest rates again has reared its ugly head. But would the Fed raise rates so close to an election? data.title: Anthropic quietly pitches its own AI safety bill to lawmakers, Politico reports
data.description:
Anthropic representatives have quietly pitched Capitol Hill lawmakers on a draft bill to regulate frontier AI safety and security, Politico reported on Friday, citing three people with knowledge of the efforts.

The bill would let the government block a model's release or use only if it poses a foreseeable, imminent risk of more than $1 billion in damages, or of killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people, according to the report.

Here are some details:

  • The risk must stem from the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model evading its developer’s controls or a cyberattack, Politico reported

  • An Anthropic spokesperson told Reuters the bill represents proposals outlined in Anthropic's "Advanced AI Framework" released earlier this year

  • The bill would grant the government the "ability to block or deter dangerous deployments of the most powerful models," and also requires developers to test frontier AI models, be transparent about findings, and get them independently evaluated, the spokesperson said

  • The Department of Commerce did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment

  • Under the bill, independent evaluators, which would register with the Commerce Department, would be tasked with periodically evaluating the lab and its frontier models, according to the report

  • The labs could pay these evaluators, provided the payment is not tied to the evaluation's outcome, the report said

  • If the evaluators determine there is “imminent enumerated risk” for a company’s frontier models, they must report it to Commerce within 72 hours of completing their assessment, Politico reported

  • While the Commerce Department could request a judge to halt a model after determining risk, the language explicitly prohibits any other US government department, agency, or officer from suspending development, deployment, or internal use, according to the report

  • A federal judge for the District Court for the District of Columbia could order the suspension of a model, the report said

data.title: Market View — Barrons.com
data.description:
This commentary was issued recently by money managers, research firms, and market newsletter writers and has been edited by Barron's.

Don't Give Up on Bonds

Perspective Capital Investment Services Sept. 30: If the bond market had a voice, we suspect it would be singing the 1970s song "Don't Give Up on Us, Baby."

Sentiment toward bonds has become so negative that we have even seen commentators describing them as among the most hated investment assets in the world.

Short-term bonds have largely avoided the carnage experienced elsewhere in the bond market. Even so, year-to-date total returns (income received plus changes in bond prices) have been flat to slightly down.

Ironically, the very rise in yields that has caused bond price declines (bond prices move inversely to yields) has also improved the future return prospects for bond investors. For shorter-term bonds, in particular, today's higher yields represent a much more attractive risk/reward proposition than witnessed in years.

Historically, current bond yield levels have been one of the strongest indicators of future bond returns. Put simply, when investors begin with higher yields, they have generally gone on to earn higher returns.

In addition to their improving risk/reward profile, we expect the higher-quality bonds we own to fulfill an important diversification role within portfolios. While no asset class works perfectly in every environment, bonds paired with durable-growth stocks can help prevent temporary stock market setbacks from becoming life-changing investment losses.

With concentration in stock markets around the world increasingly hitched to the AI-buildout wagon, diversification may prove more elusive than many investors expect. Don't give up on higher-quality bonds!

Paul A. Muzzey

Carry-Trade Risk is Growing

Commentary Centre Street Cambridge Oct. 15: The AI gamble is on view for all. But there is another, possibly larger wager that has been happening largely away from public eye: the so called "carry trade." If you can borrow money at a low rate and invest the proceeds at a higher rate, you can mint money on the difference; this is the basic business of banks. The risk lies in the possibility that the relative rates may change, making the operation unprofitable....

Another type of carry trade doesn't enjoy such safeguards, namely borrowing in the currencies of countries where rates are low, and lending or investing in countries/currencies offering higher returns. The most popular of these transactions involves the Japanese yen and the U.S. dollar. A 30-year period of a relatively stable currency vis-à-vis the dollar and interest rates of less than 1% have encouraged borrowing in yen to invest in dollars. The outstanding amount of such trades is now estimated at between $2 trillion and $3 trillion.

Unexpected shifts in exchange or interest rates can cause panic where so much money is exposed. This happened briefly in the summer of 2024. A change in central bank policy triggered a massive unloading of stocks, with the Japanese market dropping 12% in one day; the S&P 500 dropped 3%. The risks are enhanced now that Japanese economic activity has improved, and the country's interest rates are rising. A big unwinding of the carry trade could result in the sale of U.S. assets, including large amounts of Treasury securities. That would almost certainly result in higher borrowing costs and have an impact on the equity markets, as well. It is the risks we don't know that can really bite.

What's Ailing Korea's KOSPI?

Chart of the Day LPL Financial Oct. 14: The KOSPI [Korea Composite Stock Price Index] and Nasdaq Composite have generally moved in the same direction, but the magnitude of their swings has differed. Korea's market is particularly sensitive to the memory industry, leaving the KOSPI more exposed to changing sentiment surrounding DRAM and other AI-related memory products.

Both indexes staged powerful recoveries from their March lows as risk appetite returned and enthusiasm around AI accelerated. However, that concentration became a liability when AI sentiment weakened in June, contributing to a much sharper unwind in the KOSPI as crowded positioning and leverage across memory stocks reversed.

Both markets subsequently recovered, but their paths diverged over the past month. The NDX pushed to new highs as strong second-quarter earnings across the broader AI ecosystem reinforced confidence in the secular AI investment cycle. However, the KOSPI started to break down, with momentum deteriorating and the index falling back below its 200-day moving average.

Competitive concerns within the memory market have added to the pressure. China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, the fourth-largest DRAM producer, has outlined plans to begin production of new DRAM technology this year, raising concerns about additional supply and greater competition for memory leaders.

Technically, the KOSPI recently reached short-term oversold territory, but will need to reclaim its 200-day moving average and break above the August highs at 7217 to clear the way for a retest of the prior highs.
